Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 55: Program Optimization
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. Remove required work before polishing instructions
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Optimization begins with a correct reference and a workload. If a program repeatedly scans the same data, an index or precomputed summary can remove far more work than changing one instruction in the scan. But construction costs, update frequency, and memory use still count. A one-query dataset that changes constantly may favor the original scan. State which behavior must remain identical, including overflow rules and error handling, before comparing performance. This chapter separates algorithmic work counts from measured running time: fewer operations can be strong evidence for an idea, but hardware and the rest of the workload determine the actual improvement.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SP55.004: 55.1 Algorithmic optimization

2. An index replaces repeated equality tests with maintained counts
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The fixture contains two, four, two, seven, two, four. Counting each requested value with a fresh scan performs six comparisons three times, for eighteen. Building a map of counts visits the six records once; the three lookups then produce the same total of six matches. The program prints these operation counts and verifies the result. It does not measure elapsed time or claim that a map lookup costs one machine instruction. A small direct scan can still be faster because map nodes allocate memory and require pointer traversal. The useful lesson is how repeated work changes and which setup cost must be included.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SP55.022: Worked example — Reducing algorithmic work

3. Batching changes call count while preserving item order
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The baseline would send ten items with ten separate calls. Our model appends items into a batch of four, flushes each full batch, and finally flushes the remaining two. The sink receives the exact original string in order, while the number of modeled calls drops to three. The empty check in flush avoids an unnecessary fourth call. This is a batching mechanism demonstration, not a network speed measurement. A real service must also cap waiting time: if it waits forever for four items, the last two may never leave. Batch size and flush policy therefore belong to the observable latency and memory contract.

Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

4. Prefix summaries trade update cost for query cost
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The source uses half-open ranges: left is included and right is excluded. A prefix vector begins with zero, so prefix at position k means the sum of elements before k. Subtracting prefix[left] from prefix[right] then handles ordinary, full, and empty ranges with one formula. This is useful when many queries reuse stable data. If one element changes, every later prefix can become stale; the old fast query is now quickly wrong. A maintained tree or a direct scan may fit a different update pattern. Numeric bounds must also ensure the stored sums and their subtraction stay representable.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SYS55.03: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits

5. Problem and first implementation
The chapter problem

SAY
For the values 2, 4, 6, 8, answer the sum over indexes [1, 4). Precompute prefix sums so repeated range queries need two reads and a subtraction.

Begin with the complete chapter demonstration. It fixes the input so you can follow each change in state. 6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
Using prefix[right] - prefix[left + 1] accidentally drops the first requested element. Sums also need a type wide enough for the input bounds.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Build a prefix array without the leading zero but keep the same query formula. Endpoint zero and the full-range query no longer follow the stated meaning.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Define sums[k] as the total strictly before k and keep that meaning in construction, bounds, and queries.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
A leading zero makes the same subtraction work for ranges starting at zero and for empty ranges. The bounds on count and element value keep every prefix sum representable in long long. Queries borrow an already-built valid prefix vector; exposing an arbitrary editable vector is a deliberate simplification that a value type could later protect.

A plausible alternative: Optimize the repeated algorithmic work first, then measure whether lower-level changes still matter.

8. Chapter 55 — Program Optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Optimization changes an implementation while preserving its required behavior. The largest improvements often come from doing less work, moving fewer bytes, or avoiding repeated setup. Low-level instruction tuning is valuable only when the relevant instructions materially contribute to the measured bottleneck. Use a sequence of verified changes. Keep the original implementation as a reference when possible, compare outputs on normal and boundary cases, and measure each candidate under the same workload. A performance improvement that changes the result has not met the same specification. [ R2 ]

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

10. Algorithmic optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Algorithmic optimization changes the amount or organization of required work. Replacing repeated scans with an index, using a better asymptotic algorithm, or precomputing reusable summaries can dominate instruction-level changes. Account for construction and update costs. An index that makes queries fast may be inappropriate when the dataset changes constantly and only one query is performed. Optimize the complete workload, including the frequency of preprocessing and maintenance.

In plain English: First make the program correct, then measure where time is really being spent before trying to make it faster.

11. Compiler optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Compiler options enable transformations such as inlining, vectorization, and dead-code elimination. The compiler relies on language rules, available definitions, aliasing information, and target architecture. More aggressive flags can change assumptions or numerical behavior. Distinguish ordinary optimization levels from options that relax floating-point semantics or target instructions unavailable on another machine. Record the exact build configuration with results instead of describing it only as a “release build.”

In plain English: First make the program correct, then measure where time is really being spent before trying to make it faster.

12. Memory optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Memory optimization reduces allocation overhead, footprint, copying, and unnecessary lifetime extension. Reusing buffers can help when ownership is clear and retained capacity remains bounded. Do not trade a modest allocation reduction for dangling references or uncontrolled memory retention. A cache of reusable objects needs an eviction and size policy. Peak memory includes temporarily duplicated data during transformations, not merely the final representation.

In plain English: First make the program correct, then measure where time is really being spent before trying to make it faster.

13. Cache optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Cache optimization improves useful reuse and reduces transferred irrelevant bytes. Blocking, compact indexes, and traversal changes can help. The working set includes all simultaneously active data, not just the main input array. Measure the effect on total runtime and verify that a cache-focused change does not increase computation or synchronization enough to offset its benefit. Counter changes are evidence about mechanisms, not a replacement for the application’s completion metric.

In plain English: A cache is like keeping the things you use most often on your desk instead of walking to a storage room every time.

14. Reducing allocations
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Repeated small allocations can add allocator work, fragmentation, and cache misses. Reserving known capacity, using stack storage for bounded small objects, or allocating from a scoped arena can reduce those costs. Each technique changes lifetime or memory-use tradeoffs. Reserving too much wastes capacity; stack storage has size limits; arenas often reclaim everything together. Choose a mechanism whose ownership model matches the data’s actual lifetime.

15. Batching
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Batching amortizes setup, synchronization, and I/O overhead across several items. A batch can also expose vectorization or parallel work. It is especially useful when one operation has a large fixed cost relative to each item’s incremental cost. Batch size is a tuning parameter constrained by latency and memory. A service that waits indefinitely to fill a batch can harm low-volume clients. Use a maximum size and a maximum waiting policy when responsiveness matters.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

16. Data-layout optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Layout determines which fields share cache lines and how many pointers or bytes are traversed. If a hot loop reads only one eight-byte field from a 32-byte record, a separate field array can reduce the relevant data footprint from 256 KiB to 64 KiB for 8192 records in the stated layout model. That arithmetic is not a guaranteed fourfold speedup. The original layout may already be cached, other fields may be needed soon, or reconstruction costs may dominate. A layout serves operations; evaluate the complete access pattern before splitting every structure into separate arrays.

In plain English: First make the program correct, then measure where time is really being spent before trying to make it faster.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

17. Branch behavior
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Branches can be inexpensive when predictable and costly when they disrupt useful execution. Replacing a branch with arithmetic or a conditional move can help some distributions and hurt others by forcing work on both paths or creating dependencies. Benchmark representative input distributions. A test with always-true conditions does not predict behavior for irregular production data. Compiler-generated branchless code must still obey access validity; evaluating both candidate memory accesses can be unsafe when one address is invalid.

18. Prefix sums replace repeated scans
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Suppose a fixed array must answer many sum queries over half-open ranges [begin, end) . A direct scan costs work proportional to each range length. A prefix array stores prefix[k] = sum of elements before k , allowing a query to return prefix[end] - prefix[begin] after validation. For nonnegative bounded values whose total fits uint64_t , prefix construction is linear and each query is constant-time. Signed or floating-point data require additional numeric analysis: overflow and subtraction behavior must match the intended specification. Companion listing: ch55/range_sums.cpp The three query results are 45, 45, and 4500, for a combined 4590. The optimization changes repeated work from scanning every queried element to one preprocessing pass plus constant work per query. It uses extra memory and becomes less attractive when updates invalidate the prefix array frequently.

DO

19. Reducing algorithmic work
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Searching 1,000 queries by rescanning a 1,000,000-element array performs on the order of a billion comparisons. Building an index once can reduce each later lookup dramatically. Changing the algorithm often dominates instruction-level tuning because it removes whole classes of work rather than making each iteration slightly cheaper.

20. Structure-of-arrays example
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
If a loop processes only x coordinates from records containing x,y,z,color,metadata , an array-of-structures layout fetches unused neighboring fields into cache lines. Separating frequently processed x values into their own dense array can increase useful bytes per cache line, at the cost of more complex organization for operations that need complete records.

24. Compiler options are part of the experiment’s contract
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A compiler can inline calls, combine operations, remove dead work, or vectorize a loop when the language rules permit it. The source loop need not look the same in assembly. But some options change assumptions, such as allowing less strict floating-point transformations or requiring instructions unavailable on older processors. An apparent improvement may therefore come with changed results or portability. Record the complete relevant build configuration and verify the required outputs under it. A release label alone does not identify the program being measured. Fix undefined behavior rather than treating one favorable optimized result as a guarantee.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SP55.006: 55.2 Compiler optimization

------------------------------------------------------------

25. Layout should serve the fields a hot loop actually uses
Reason about the implementation

SAY
The source layout model considers eight thousand one hundred ninety-two records of thirty-two bytes each, while a hot pass reads only one eight-byte field. The complete records occupy two hundred fifty-six kibibytes; the isolated field array occupies sixty-four. That is a footprint calculation, not a guaranteed fourfold speedup. The original data may already be cached, other fields may be needed by the next operation, and splitting records can complicate ownership and updates. Compare the full access pattern before changing layout. Useful bytes per transfer can explain a measurement, but does not replace the application's completion metric.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SP55.016: 55.7 Data-layout optimization

------------------------------------------------------------

26. Allocation reduction creates new lifetime choices
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Repeated small allocations can add overhead, but each replacement technique changes the lifetime model. Reserving a known vector capacity can reduce reallocations while still requiring a sensible upper bound. Reusing a buffer avoids acquisition work but may retain a huge capacity after one unusual request. A scoped arena makes many allocations cheap and reclaims them together, which fits only when their lifetimes can end together. Do not keep raw observers into storage that a later growth or arena reset invalidates. An optimization should make the required ownership clearer, not save allocation calls by introducing dangling references.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SP55.012: 55.5 Reducing allocations

------------------------------------------------------------

27. Branch removal can perform work that the branch avoided
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A branch that is almost always taken can be cheaper than calculating both possible results. For irregular input, a different arrangement may help the processor, but only measurement can establish that for the actual distribution. More seriously, rewriting a guarded load into two unconditional loads can access an invalid address even if a later selection discards its value. Source-level validity comes before branch-count reduction. Compare representative input patterns and inspect what the compiler generates rather than assuming a conditional expression is automatically branchless or faster. The cost belongs to the resulting dependency and memory behavior, not the spelling alone.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

31. Remove repeated work before tuning instructions
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Remove repeated work before tuning instructions. The loop stores the sum of the first i+1 values at prefix[i+1]. The leading zero makes empty prefixes valid. Each value is added once during construction.

For the values 2, 4, 6, 8, answer the sum over indexes [1, 4). Precompute prefix sums so repeated range queries need two reads and a subtraction.

prefix[k] means the sum of values before index k. The half-open endpoints match the prefix definition. All terms before the left endpoint cancel.

The loop stores the sum of the first i+1 values at prefix[i+1]. The leading zero makes empty prefixes valid. Each value is added once during construction.

For the half-open index interval [1,4), subtract the sum before index one from the sum before index four. This returns 4+6+8=18 without rescanning the range.

prefix[k] contains the sum of values before index k. A valid half-open query [a,b) returns prefix[b] minus prefix[a].

Using prefix[right] - prefix[left + 1] accidentally drops the first requested element. Sums also need a type wide enough for the input bounds. In the extended lab: Build a prefix array without the leading zero but keep the same query formula. Endpoint zero and the full-range query no longer follow the stated meaning.

42. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
A leading zero makes the same subtraction work for ranges starting at zero and for empty ranges. The bounds on count and element value keep every prefix sum representable in long long. Queries borrow an already-built valid prefix vector; exposing an arbitrary editable vector is a deliberate simplification that a value type could later protect.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Optimize the repeated algorithmic work first, then measure whether lower-level changes still matter.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Build a prefix array without the leading zero but keep the same query formula. Endpoint zero and the full-range query no longer follow the stated meaning. Define sums[k] as the total strictly before k and keep that meaning in construction, bounds, and queries.

43. Optimization verification needs adversarial equivalence cases
Recall and transfer

SAY
An optimized implementation should be compared with a straightforward reference across cases that expose different behavior. Empty ranges catch off-by-one assumptions. Large allowed values test arithmetic bounds. Invalid ranges test error contracts. If the optimization caches summaries, mutate the underlying data and verify the documented invalidation or update path. A performance run on one all-positive fixture can miss a wrong subtraction, stale index, or different rejection rule. Keep correctness checks separate from the timing interval when appropriate, but do not remove them from the experiment. Faster wrong answers do not satisfy the same workload.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

content/systems-programming/ch55.json → SP55.026: Guided lab and review

------------------------------------------------------------

44. Accept an optimization only with its full tradeoff
Recall and transfer

SAY
A useful optimization review names the removed work and the new costs. The frequency index eliminates repeated scans but adds construction and storage. Batching reduces call count but changes waiting and buffering. A compact layout can reduce irrelevant memory traffic but complicate operations that need full records. These are concrete tradeoffs, not reasons to reject optimization. State the workload where the change helps, verify equivalence, measure the chosen boundary, and document any new invariants. If the input distribution or update frequency changes later, maintainers should know which assumption to re-evaluate before preserving an old optimization by habit.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.
